lessons.canDo: Describe how innate defenses spot and flag a threat
lessons.description: Learn how early immune defenses notice common signs of microbes or injury without identifying a particular germ.

screens.brief: You scrape your knee. Before your body knows whether any germ entered, what might tell it something is wrong?
screens.visual: A small scrape in the skin, with nearby cells shown beneath it.

screens.brief: Some immune cells stationed in tissues act like watchguards. They look for signs of trouble rather than the name of a particular germ.
screens.visual: A watchguard immune cell beside ordinary tissue cells.

screens.brief: One sign is a feature shared by many microbes, like a recognizable part of their outer surface. It is more like spotting a familiar uniform than reading someone's name tag.
screens.visual: Two different-looking microbes with the same outer feature highlighted.

screens.brief: Ask which clue a watchguard could notice early: a shared feature on several bacteria or the exact name of one bacterium. Include the exact name as the tempting wrong answer.
Injured body cells can also give off signs of damage, even when no microbe is present. Like a smoke alarm, the watchguard can notice trouble without knowing its exact cause.
screens.visual: An injured cell and a microbe, each with a different sign pointing toward the same watchguard cell.

screens.brief: When a watchguard detects one of these signs, it can warn nearby cells. The warning flags a possible threat; it does not prove which germ, if any, is there.
screens.visual: A watchguard cell sending a simple warning signal to neighboring cells.

screens.brief: Ask which situations could trigger an early warning: a cut with damaged cells, a microbe with a recognizable outer feature, or only a germ whose exact identity is known. Include 'only a germ whose exact identity is known' as the tempting wrong answer.

While gardening, you get a small splinter and notice the skin around it has been hurt. Ask what an early watchguard might detect and why it could warn nearby cells before knowing whether a germ entered.
screens.visual: A splinter breaking the skin, with nearby injured cells and a watchguard cell.

skills.description: Innate defenses notice shared signs of microbes or damaged cells and can warn nearby cells without identifying a particular germ.
skills.example: A watchguard immune cell notices damaged cells beside a splinter and sends a warning.
skills.name: Explain how innate defenses detect and flag threats
skills.useCase: Understanding why your body can react quickly when you scrape your skin.

lessons.title: Innate immune detection
